https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/j.text: 0:43 Police footage shows scale of damage inside Aeon mall after explosion cause by Japan quake – video Japan Death toll in Japan earthquake rises to 30 as aftershock and heat hamper rescue efforts Soldiers and emergency teams search damaged shopping centre, paper mill and homes for survivors Earthquake rocks southern Japanese island of Kyushu – in pictures Gavin Blair in Tokyo Thu 30 Jul 2026 02.49 EDT First published on Wed 29 Jul 2026 22.09 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The death toll from the powerful earthquake that hit Japan on Tuesday has risen to 30, as the search for survivors trapped in a badly damaged shopping centre, paper mill and collapsed homes across the south-west of the country continues. ‘The shaking was terrifying’: stories of survival and loss emerge after Japan earthquake Read more The 6.8-magnitude quake, which struck Kumamoto prefecture on the island of Kyushu, injured at least 62 people, according to the prefectural government. Almost 5,000 Self-Defence Forces (SDF) personnel deployed to the region faced temperatures of up to 35C on Thursday, officials said, adding that a 5.8-magnitude aftershock overnight had further hampered the rescue efforts. Map of earthquake site About 170 rescue workers were searching the Aeon shopping centre in the town of Kashima, which was bustling with thousands of people when the quake struck. The company said about 3,000 customers were evacuated to a car park before a gas explosion occurred in another part of the shopping centre. Six of the 12 people pulled from the rubble have died. All those caught in the explosion were shop workers who had returned to the building after the evacuation, Aeon said. The company’s president bowed in apology at a press conference on Wednesday, saying Aeon had failed to anticipate the explosion, the cause of which was being investigated. 1:09 Aerial footage shows collapsed buildings after 6.8 magnitude Japan earthquake – video Japanese media footage from inside the shopping centre showed part of the ceiling had collapsed, with metal fragments and other debris scattered across the floor as helmeted, masked rescue workers searched the area. Police and SDF personnel were continuing to search for one worker in the debris at the Nippon Paper mill in Yatsushiro, where a chimney collapsed. Of the 10 others who were trapped, eight died and two were injured. In the first reported death of a foreign national, a Vietnamese technical intern was killed after a crane fell on him at the factory where he worked, according to the Vietnamese government. View image in fullscreen Nippon Paper mill, where a chimney collapsed. Photograph: Jiji Press/EPA Nearly 23,000 homes had no electricity and 75,000 had no running water, Kumamoto officials said. About 15,000 people had been evacuated to 400 shelters. The defence minister said on Wednesday evening that the SDF was airlifting coolers to shelters in Kumamoto, while SDF vessels were delivering water and food. “We’re doing everything possible to make saving lives a priority, making efforts to deliver life-saving supplies, beginning with water,” Shinjiro Koizumi said. Aerial police footage showed several homes had been flattened, including some that had crumbled into a river. View image in fullscreen A collapsed house in Hikawa, Kumamoto. Photograph: Kyodo/Reuters The earthquake registered the maximum level 7 on Japan’s seven-level shindo scale. “It was the strongest quake I have ever experienced,” Kanzo Matsumoto, 73, the operator of a luxury hot spring inn in Yatsushiro, told Agence France-Presse. The national Geospatial Information Authority said parts of the ground had shifted by 87cm during the quake. Yatsushiro town hall sustained damage to its base-isolation system, an earthquake-resistant technology designed to protect buildings by cushioning their foundations against intense shaking. The system was rebuilt after a deadly earthquake in 2016. View image in fullscreen Vehicles are crushed under collapsed buildings in Yatsushiro, south-western Japan. Photograph: Hiro Komae/AP Some car and semiconductor manufacturers with plants in Kyushu have halted production. Toyota said it would pause operations at three plants while it assessed the quake’s impact on suppliers and ⁠logistics. Honda suspended operations at a motorcycle plant until Friday. Taiwan’s TSMC has resumed operations at its Kumamoto facility, while Sony, Renesas Electronics and Tokyo Electron have halted production. Kyushu is ‌an important hub for Japan’s automotive and semiconductor industries, which account for about 20% of the region’s industrial output. Analysts said the shutdowns appeared to be driven largely by precaution than damage to production facilities. Kumamoto was struck by two devastating earthquakes in 2016 that killed 273 people and injured more than 2,800.The archipelago, home to about 125 million people, usually experiences hundreds of jolts every year and accounts for about 18% of the world’s earthquakes. https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text: Rescue work continues in the aftermath of catastrophic flooding in Nepal and Tibet. News sites have been hit by racist comments about missing Australians. Photograph: Arun Sankar/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Rescue work continues in the aftermath of catastrophic flooding in Nepal and Tibet. News sites have been hit by racist comments about missing Australians. Photograph: Arun Sankar/AFP/Getty Images Nepal-Tibet flood disaster Australians missing in Nepal targeted by ‘heartbreaking’ and ‘abhorrent’ racist slurs As families await news after the catastrophe, community members appeal for compassion in the face of hateful rhetoric Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Caitlin Cassidy and Kat Wong Mon 31 Aug 2026 02.32 EDT Last modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 03.37 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A slew of racist social media comments have been made towards Australians missing in the catastrophic Nepal-Tibet floods , prompting calls for greater accountability of major platforms to remove hateful rhetoric. On Monday, the total number of Australians missing after flash floods triggered by a massive glacier collapse in the Himalayas rose to 43, and the overall death toll was at least 810 people. Most of the missing Australians were on pilgrimages , including to Mount Kailash in Tibet, which is a sacred site for Hindus, Buddhists, Jains and followers of the Bon faith. Fourteen are Sydney-based members of the Australia Bharatha Brahmin Samaj community. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email As families and friends face an agonising wait to learn the fate of their loved ones, mainstream media outlets including News Corp, Channel 7, Channel 10 and Nine have been hit with highly offensive and discriminatory comments on Facebook articles identifying the missing Australians in Nepal. Some outlets, including Guardian Australia, have limited who can comment on posts about the missing tourists after receiving strings of racist replies on social media. One Daily Telegraph article received dozens of comments on Facebook from people claiming that missing citizens who were not white weren’t Australian, which were later deleted. One said: “Hoping we have new vacancies in Australia that Aussies can fill.” The outlet’s editor, Ben English, said the comments on the post were “abhorrent” and “have no place on our platforms”. “We are responsible for the comment threads on our pages and we take that responsibility seriously … But no automated filter reliably catches racism expressed in coded language,” he said. Rescue efforts continue as 43 Australians remain missing in Nepal – video “Where we cannot actively moderate a thread on a sensitive story, we will close it – and we have moved to do that here.” The comments have also proliferated on X. One post by conservative commentator Kobie Thatcher, who wrote “Aussie family” in quotation marks alongside an image of an identified missing couple, was viewed 3.2m times. Associate Prof at QUT’s Digital Media Research Centre, Tim Graham, said hateful rhetoric had been increasing on social media platforms for the past decade. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion Nepal-Tibet floods: rescuers race to reach 900 people believed trapped in hydropower tunnels Read more “The design architecture of these websites, the algorithms that they use to curate content and put it into feeds, rewards this kind of stuff,” he said. “It brings out the worst in people, but it also plays into the political economy of these platforms where rage bait, extreme content or borderline content … attracts so much attention.” He said platforms had the technical infrastructure and the resources to push back against harmful content, including generative AI models that could detect “nuanced content at scale”, but weren’t using it for moderation. “I really don’t understand why that can’t be applied in special circumstances to a really terrible humanitarian catastrophe like this,” he said. “It’s a bit mind-boggling.” The race discrimination commissioner, Giridharan Sivaraman, said he wasn’t surprised by the comments, which he connected to Australia’s current debate on migrants. “They’re saying, you don’t deserve to … be seen as Australian. And that’s amplified by the rhetoric of far-right populist parties,” he said. “We should be very concerned because it’s indicative of a real rise in white supremacy ideology … Words have consequences … It’s heartbreaking.” Sivaraman said racism was “profitable” for social media companies, and the notion they were attempting to stop hate speech on their platforms was “fanciful”. “This is just more evidence as to why we need a digital duty of care for all social media platforms that operate in Australia,” he said. Hindu Council of Australia vice-president Surinder Jain said it was “saddening” to see people making use of a tragedy to “express their displeasure with the government”. “I … ask them to show some dignity to those who have perished and the families of those who are mourning their loss: give them a fair go,” he told Guardian Australia. Australia’s Indian diaspora, which includes Hindus, has been the target of racist comments from far-right movements including March for Australia as immigration has emerged as a hot-button issue. Nepalese Australian Welfare Society president, Chiran Tiwari, said Australians needed to look past nationalities and have humanity. “It is very hurtful and the families who are impacted feel really, really bad,” he told Guardian Australia. “All of us are human.” Explore more on these topics Nepal-Tibet flood disaster Social media Australian media Digital media news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

https://www.politico.eu/article/macron-s.text: PARIS — French President Emmanuel Macron on Wednesday hit out at the “unacceptable and stupid comments from many foreign leaders” in the aftermath of unrest which rocked several French cities over the weekend. “Some people have claimed that we’ve been overrun by hordes of migrants and Islamists, which is completely false,” Macron told reporters during a trip to Qatar. His comments were a clear swipe at U.S. President Donald Trump, who this week railed that France is “being conquered, looted, and burned to the ground by migrants, jihadists, and Communists.” While hundreds of thousands of protesters in France demonstrated peacefully over the cost of living and school conditions at the weekend, the mayhem — including public buildings being set on fire, stores being looted and clashes with riot police — sparked widespread condemnation in France and abroad, including in the U.S., where Trump is using the French unrest to rally voters ahead of November’s midterm elections. Advertisement Advertisement There is no evidence tying last weekend’s incidents in France to immigration. Macron said Trump is “among” a group of political leaders who are campaigning “off of France’s back,” adding, “it’s at times like these that you can tell who loves France and who doesn’t.” Right-leaning leaders in other European countries like Hungary and Poland also tried to pin the unrest in France on immigration to justify their countries’ hard-line policies on the divisive issue. Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar said on X that the chaos that engulfed several French cities makes it “clear to everyone why Hungary advocates the strictest possible approach to migration.” French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot responded by offering to “assist the countries concerned in understanding the situation, to prevent them from spreading or relaying false information.” “Foreign leaders who comment on or exploit recent events in France for electoral purposes or to harm us — without understanding anything about them — should show at least a basic measure of restraint,” he added.

https://24.hu/tudomany/2026/11/11/uj-kin.text: A kínai nagy fal eddig ismeretlen szakaszát fedezték fel régészek Pekingben. A város önkormányzatának közleménye szerint ez az első alkalom, hogy a Szuj-dinasztia korából származó falromokat tártak fel a településen. A szakemberek egy mintegy 800 négyzetméteres területen végeztek feltárást 2026 augusztusa és októbere között, Csangping kerületben. A munkálatok során több mint 60 leletre bukkantak rá, köztük porcelánokra, pénzérmékre, fegyverekre és mindennapi használati tárgyakra. Ezek az időszámításunk szerinti 4. és 13. század közöttről származnak, magát a falszakaszt viszont csak a Szuj-dinasztia idején (581–618) építették. Ez az első alkalom, hogy a Szuj-dinasztia korából származó nagyfal-maradványokat fedeztek fel Peking térségében. A lelet nagy jelentőséggel bír a pekingi nagy fal építési időrendjének, elhelyezkedésének, tájolásának és katonai védelmi rendszerének kutatása szempontjából – idézi a közlemény San Heng kutatót, a Pekingi Régészeti Intézet munkatársát. A kínai nagy fal nem egyetlen korszakban épült, sőt még csak nem is összefüggő építmény. Különböző államok és dinasztiák évszázadokon keresztül építettek új falszakaszokat, illetve restauráltak és bővített ki meglévőket – jegyzi meg a Heritage Daily . A Szuj-dinasztia előtt az Északi Csi-dinasztia kiterjedt határvédelmi erődítményeket emelt Észak-Kína területén. A Szuj-dinasztia később fenntartotta és tovább bővítette ezeket a védelmi rendszereket, hogy biztosítsa a birodalom északi határvidékét. További régészeti híreink alább olvashatók:
